Left a do-not-re-litigate note explaining why the previous design was deliberate, so the next person does not undo the reasoning by accident.
follow_up_detail: He preserved production secrets during the deploy by pushing cell by cell through the platform's command-line tool rather than a project import, which wipes credentials — a gotcha he had documented earlier and applied here.
The validation checkpoint was scheduled with an automated report and a stated failure signal, rather than declaring victory at deploy.
The remaining empty views after launch were all correctly explained — reps with no allocation on a new roster, not a filter fault — which is the distinction between a bug and an expected state.

In the same session he closed an unrelated leak: disqualified records were filtered only at add time, so a number of them lingered. He added a real-time filter, a reclaim path in the reconciliation, and a one-time cleanup.

stories.title: Ported five fragile notebooks into a versioned platform
stories.situation: Commission calculation for six teams ran on five unversioned notebooks. Manual adjustments required hand-editing warehouse queries. The data lead had flagged the write-back path as lacking transactional controls.
stories.task: Port everything to a real codebase without silently changing anyone's pay.
stories.action: The method is the accomplishment: every phase was validated against a historical fixture from the old system, and every single row difference had to be *explained*, not tolerated. One runner came back with no missing rows and a handful of extras, each attributed to legitimate drift — a roster addition, releases after the cutoff, deliberately skipped items. Another had a missing row traced to a type change on one specific opportunity. A third matched exactly, the only difference being integer-versus-float representation. He also refactored the source-of-truth spreadsheet structurally before porting the code, merging three parallel definition tabs into one with a scope schema so a single join handles every scoping rule.
key_decisions: Used historical fixtures as the correctness contract rather than testing against expected behavior, because the requirement was 'nobody's pay changes silently' and only a real comparison proves that.

Chose a spreadsheet as the operational database *deliberately* rather than transitionally, and wrote down both the reasoning and the revisit triggers: at this scale the API limits do not bite, operators including a non-engineer covering during leave can inspect and edit the source of truth directly — which is a feature — and a future migration changes the read-write layer rather than the data shape.
Stated the principle that settles it: the storage decision is reversible, the permissions philosophy is not. Get the permissions right and the storage can move later.
Named three specific conditions that would trigger revisiting it, rather than leaving the choice as a matter of taste.
Deliberately broke a legacy generator when migrating the definition tabs, and said so, rather than maintaining two readers.
follow_up_detail: He caught his own arithmetic error during the port and corrected it: the documentation described a payout as multiplying by a tier rate, but the actual formula also multiplies by the rep's normal base rate — the accelerator pays an extra tier-rate of normal commission per over-quota dollar.

He caught a systematic off-by-one in the pay-cycle convention that had a quarterly runner firing in the wrong months, and turned it into a standing rule plus a first-action-of-every-session orientation step, because he had seen it produce a wrong conclusion in a prior document.
He built recurring safeguards into the pipeline rather than the runbook — an audit that runs automatically before publish, and an adjustments module with idempotent preview and apply.

He later replaced part of his own architecture after using it: a per-month code module for corrections was unnecessary indirection for routine work, so he built an inline form that persists to the same file and drains through the identical apply machinery — not a parallel path, a different front door onto the same one — while enumerating exactly when the original is still the right choice.

stories.title: Wrote his own mandate and asked to be told what was not his
stories.situation: He was functioning as the de-facto revenue-operations lead with no published scope. Reporting work overlapping his was appearing from adjacent functions without handoffs, platform execution lived elsewhere while he was informally the business-side owner, and the boundary with the executive dashboard kept shifting. He had received signals that he was operating outside his lane.
stories.task: Turn a diffuse frustration into a document his manager could act on.
stories.action: He led with observations rather than asks. Three of them: the work required to hit the stated sales objective is scattered across multiple functions with nobody accountable for the outcome, so each person does their own interpretation of what helps. Churn is treated reactively — by the time it appears in a dashboard the account has already drifted — backed by his own finding that most of the managed book had no open renewal opportunity and that team-level gross retention was being masked by expansion in the headline number. And the administrative burden on sellers keeps being solved one instance at a time when it is a category. Then he diagnosed the blockers as system problems rather than people problems, and made a request most people do not make.
key_decisions: Asked leadership to tell him what was *not* his: 'for each of these, what's the right home? I'd rather have one clear lane than a fuzzy claim on all of it.'
Read the outside-your-lane signal as a symptom rather than a rebuke — 'I take those seriously, and I read them as me making priority calls in a vacuum, not me actually overreaching.'
Named the invisible tradeoff directly: saying yes to one request is implicitly saying no to another, and that arithmetic is not visible to the person asking.

Made the governance ask conditional and named its failure mode up front — a rubric only works if leadership will engage when something gets deprioritized. 'If you're up for that, I'll build it. If not, I'd rather know now than spend cycles on governance that won't get respected.'
Diagnosed fragmentation without blaming anyone: 'the output looks incoherent — not because anyone is doing bad work, but because no one is integrating it.'
follow_up_detail: The memo enumerated the full actual scope across three categories — operational, data and analytics, and strategy and design — which made the size of the undefined role visible rather than arguable.

He paired it with a proposed organizational structure and co-authored a split between revenue operations and platform engineering: one owns strategy, policy and judgment, the other owns build, automation and integration.
He stated the capacity reality plainly rather than absorbing it — the current team cannot execute even one major priority effectively.

A self-observation from the same period that says something about how he works: 'I was so excited by how much faster I could get things done with AI that I finally paused to think — okay, I can do stuff a lot faster, but that doesn't mean I can do everything immediately. I still have finite hours in the day.'
He was subsequently handed ownership of the cross-functional coordination meeting and redefined its attendee list.

stories.title: Built the rubric that decides what gets worked on
stories.situation: Every cross-functional request competed equally for his time, and he had no published frame to point at when pushing back. He had named the gap himself in a memo to his manager: priority calls were being made in a vacuum, which is what made them look arbitrary from outside.
stories.task: Build the governance he had asked permission to build.
stories.action: He wrote a mission statement for the function and a priority scale scored on one thing only — revenue impact, counting both top-line growth and churn reduction — mapped directly onto the ticketing system's priority field so the scoring lands where the work already lives rather than in a separate document. Each level carries a threshold and a pattern rather than a vague description: the top level is a direct multi-million-dollar move or a systemic compounding effect, such as a decision gating an org-wide program or a system a double-digit number of reps use daily. The bottom level is reactive administration with no revenue thread, and he made it a real bucket rather than a polite fiction.
key_decisions: Scored on revenue impact only, with explicit anti-patterns: do not score on effort, do not score on complexity, do not score on stakeholder pressure.
Forbade reactive re-scoring — a priority moves only when scope changes materially, not when someone complains about where their request landed.
Wrote the anti-pattern against padding: the lowest bucket is real, and inflating items into a higher one to feel productive defeats the instrument.
Built it into the daily selection ritual rather than leaving it as a document — highest priority first, ties broken by staleness — so it is used every morning rather than cited occasionally.
Stated the purpose in one line: converting 'Joe decided' into 'the system decided.'
follow_up_detail: The application procedure is specific: score on creation, capture the reasoning in one sentence, and on a material scope change add a comment recording the old and new priority with the reason — so the audit trail lives with the work.
It doubles as the pushback instrument: if a request does not clear the middle threshold, it queues behind anything that does, and the conversation is about the rubric rather than about him.
He applied it to existing tickets the same day rather than leaving it aspirational.
It reads as the answer to two questions a planning role will always ask — how do you prioritize, and what happens when your read contradicts what a leader wants.

stories.title: Designed the hiring bar for his own counterpart
stories.situation: The company was hiring a revenue-operations manager to partner with him — effectively a second version of his own role — on a short timeline, run jointly with Finance and a recruiter.
stories.task: Design a screen and an assessment that actually discriminate, in a market where AI makes a polished deliverable table stakes.
stories.action: He made an uncomfortable trade explicitly and wrote it down: technical and AI proficiency is the *bar*, and operational strength is the *differentiator* — the dimension where this hire should be stronger than he is. Strong operations with weak technical does not advance, stated as a decision rather than left as a judgment call. He wrote the screen to be self-contained for a non-technical screener with deeper probes tagged for himself and Finance, and built the questions around falsifiable signals: the AI question asks for the last thing the candidate actually built or shipped and lists the vocabulary a real user emits, treating the absence of a verification story as a red flag rather than neutral. The take-home was built from a real internal project, anonymized with synthetic data and deliberately messy — several raw files from two systems, no data dictionary.
key_decisions: Planted a marquee trap that is a judgment test rather than a puzzle: a set of records where neither an identifier join nor a fuzzy name match reconnects them, and the clean key is the billing email. Fuzzy matching is the obstacle, not the intended solution.

Made the consequence the point rather than the trap: miss it and you classify a large group of known, often-contracted accounts as unbound and repriceable — the exact error that has real customer consequences.

Made the headline number the single most diagnostic signal: a naive read of one revenue column against true paying revenue differ materially, and where a candidate lands — and whether they can explain why — is the assessment.

Calibrated the case by running it fresh through isolated AI models to see which traps a machine clears unassisted. The frontier model produced a complete, reproducible answer and still missed the marquee trap; the mid-tier model produced artifacts that did not reconcile with each other.
Drew the conclusion that shaped the rubric: model tier sets the polish floor, so polish is not signal — the candidate's judgment is, and both tiers missed the trap unprompted.
follow_up_detail: He simplified the case mid-build when a construct got in the way, and when he realized the change had only been applied to the shared copy he went back and matched the source — retaining an unused random draw so the same seed still reproduces the published dataset exactly.
He graded a real finalist against it with the same discipline, wrote the exact live probe that would decide the outcome, and named her ceiling if she defended the wrong answer.
He weighted her strengths honestly too: her financial model tied across every artifact, which is precisely what the mid-tier calibration baseline had failed.

The AI-enablement pillar of the job description is his own teaching initiative turned into a role requirement, and one screen question grades for hands-on measured adoption while marking a one-and-done training session as a red flag.

stories.title: Turned a reporting bottleneck into distributed capability
stories.situation: Every recurring reporting request routed through him. Non-technical colleagues across customer success, implementation and sales management had no way to build anything themselves.
stories.task: Turn a one-person bottleneck into capability distributed across teams.
stories.action: He started informally and dated it honestly, including a note to himself about not overclaiming — a practitioner beginning to bring others along, not the operator of a deployed program, with an instruction to soften the claim if it stalled. Then he ran a hands-on session where each attendee built their own real working application rather than watching a demo: a review app for one colleague, a data app for another, a calculator for a third. He shipped a three-part video series the same afternoon so the session was reusable rather than a one-off, framed to make it feel achievable — a working app in about fifteen minutes of typing plus fifteen minutes of waiting.
key_decisions: Made attendees build rather than watch, because a demo produces admiration and a build produces capability.
Shipped the follow-up videos the same day, while the session was still fresh and before the momentum decayed.

Cleared the actual blocker himself rather than assigning it — chased read-only warehouse provisioning for attendees, and established the cost fact that unblocked the request, that the warehouse bills per query rather than per user so read access carries no ongoing cost.
Tied it to his own scope with a stated reason: enabling others to build their own solutions is what frees him to focus on where leadership actually wants him.
Kept the claim honest in his own job-search materials, with an explicit instruction to remove the hook if the initiative did not take.
follow_up_detail: The adoption compounded visibly — a senior stakeholder reported building an automation of their own, unprompted, off the back of the session.
He demonstrated the notebook-building workflow to the growth analyst separately so she could generate dashboards the same way.
He seeded a company-wide conversation about bot and agent sprawl, which pulled in the owner of roughly ten live bots and produced a router design discussion — with him as convener rather than owner.
Enablement became one of the named functions in his mandate memo and a pillar of the role he was hiring for, which is the difference between an initiative and a durable change.

stories.title: Refused to hide the mess in a handoff
stories.situation: He was handing five recurring, business-critical processes to four people before a six-week leave: monthly commissions across six teams, deal desk, the monthly business review, the leadership forecast meeting, and a live price-increase program.
stories.task: Make each one runnable by someone else.
stories.action: He rejected his own too-clean first draft. His words: we need to be super honest about the open next steps I have not tackled — the price increases are definitely the biggest mess I will be leaving behind. The reasoning became a durable rule: a handoff that hides the mess is worse than none, because the person covering needs the truth. One document per area, one named owner per area, matched to function rather than availability. Each document opens with a blunt state-at-handoff section rather than an idealized process description. The commissions document was written for a finance person rather than an engineer — plain language, technical asides explicitly marked skippable, every formula given a worked example with real numbers so she could check the math herself.
key_decisions: Matched owners to function rather than to who had capacity, and named a single escalation owner for time-sensitive decisions so nobody would wait on him.

Set an explicit default posture rather than leaving judgment ambiguous: follow the documented process; if it is a new decision, log it and route it rather than improvising something new during the leave.

Included an explicit unknown-confirm-before-relying-on section listing genuine open questions, including a contradiction between his own newer note and older documentation which he disclosed rather than papered over.

Made a scoping call that unblocked his successor: a large reconciliation effort is a soft gate rather than a wall — only a specific small set must be corrected before the next wave, the rest runs in parallel.
Solved the access problem structurally rather than by sharing credentials, adding a co-owner across every repository so the work could be run and maintained without him.
follow_up_detail: He gave permission along with the process, for a gap he could not close: there is no system of record for *why* a compensation change happened, and that context lived in messages he would not have access to. So he set the precedent explicitly — it is completely normal to verify by searching your own history, and a missing paper trail is not a blocker.
The commissions document lists eight named mistakes learned the hard way, each with the symptom, so the reader recognizes them rather than rediscovering them.

It teaches distinctions rather than steps — two different quarterly and monthly artifacts that both get casually called the same thing, and which months a quarterly process correctly does *not* run, so a skipped run reads as expected rather than as a bug.
Closing precedence rule: where the code and a document disagree, the code wins; where you are unsure, the escalation owner wins.

stories.title: Redistributed a departed rep’s book, and balanced the bad work too
stories.situation: A seller was deactivated, leaving dozens of open opportunities and well over a thousand accounts unowned. His manager wanted full coverage so the customer-facing team would have someone to contact on every account.
stories.task: Redistribute cleanly.
stories.action: He preferred continuity over even distribution, in a stated tier order: current account owner first, then prior opportunity owner on the account, then anyone appearing in the account's ownership history, then anyone with recent activity on it, and only then a round-robin. Late-stage opportunities prefer senior sellers within their tier, with soft and hard caps on how many any one person receives. He measured how much signal actually existed and reported it honestly — fewer than half the opportunities had any continuity signal at all, so the rest were genuinely arbitrary and he said so rather than implying the algorithm knew more than it did.
key_decisions: Tracked and balanced the *stale* work separately from the fresh work — many of the opportunities had close dates well past, meaning they create hygiene work rather than selling opportunity, and letting the rotation land them wherever it happened to land would have dumped all of it on one or two people.

Refused to let staleness override real continuity: if someone has genuine history with an account, they get it even if all of it is stale. Fairness in the cleanup does not outrank knowing the customer.
Bucketed the accounts by whether coverage was actually needed — real customers routed through the same tiered logic, prospects flipped to a house owner with no active coverage.
Suppressed notifications on the coverage backfill deliberately, because a backfill is not an actionable handoff and notifying on it trains people to ignore notifications.
Raised three caveats to the manager rather than silently deciding them, including two opportunities whose type normally routes to a different team entirely.
follow_up_detail: The result of the stale-balancing choice, stated as a check: every seller received a small comparable number of stale items rather than one person receiving all of them.
He flagged a sequencing risk nobody else would have caught — do not reassign until the departing rep's final commission cycle is locked, or movement on these opportunities distorts his final payment.
He verified after execution rather than trusting the run: full match on the customer accounts, a sampled match on the prospects, and a direct check that the departed rep owned zero records.
He used an execution pattern validated on a prior smaller move — single-record updates so the organization's automations fire per record — rather than a bulk path that would have skipped them.

project_archetypes.title: Forward ARR landing forecast from open pipeline
project_archetypes.description: A monthly ending-ARR forecast built as a recursive movement bridge — prior month's book, less churn and contraction, plus expansion, reactivation, promotional roll-off, and new business. Current open pipeline is weighted by a point-in-time win-probability model built to replace the CRM's stage-based probability, which materially overstated what open pipeline was worth. Churn is a customer-level monthly hazard model, which buys a defensible non-flat shape driven by the renewal calendar plus an account-level at-risk worklist Customer Success can act on. Every component method was chosen by walk-forward backtest rather than preference, and lumpy months winsorized so a single outlier deal can't set the trend. Delivered as a three-scenario cone where each scenario is a regime the business has actually been in, not an arbitrary shock — tight near-term, fanning out with horizon.

project_archetypes.title: Bookings-to-billings translation
project_archetypes.description: Signed ARR and billed ARR are different numbers, and the gap between them was going unexplained. Built the booked-to-billed funnel: compared every recent booking against what it is actually invoicing, then classified each gap account into documented attrition (a contraction or churn record exists), still in implementation (expected — not billing yet), or silent leakage (no record anywhere). Only the third bucket is a process failure, and separating it changed the conversation from a scary aggregate number to a specific, actionable list. Established the revenue realization curve underneath it: non-payroll revenue lands essentially at signature, payroll ramps from roughly half of steady-state at month zero to full run-rate around month five as employees onboard — so booked revenue arrives as billings over months. Codified the canonical billed-ARR definition (provisioning-based) against the bookings definition so exec reporting stops conflating them.

project_archetypes.title: Deal Desk Agent — agentic deal review in Slack
project_archetypes.description: A Slack-native agent that gives sellers an instant, trustworthy answer on whether a deal clears the bar. A rep drops a CRM quote link into a channel; the agent reads the quote, rolls individual SKUs up to their current package, computes gross margin against a cost model derived from a trailing-twelve-month allocation (never hardcoded rates), and replies in-thread — pass, or fail plus the specific price change that would clear it. Three deterministic arms: is the margin right, is the quote structurally built right (required fields, deal-type consistency, co-termination, date sanity), and is it the right package and entitlement for this customer. The core design commitment is deterministic verdict, LLM shell: the math is Python and gets relayed verbatim, so the model orchestrates and explains but never guesses a number. Shipped as a custom MCP server (~16 tools) running as a hosted connector behind a Slack agent, with read-only CRM access, promo-aware margin logic so a sanctioned promotion isn't read as a margin failure, and channel-aware output that fails closed — full cost and margin figures surface only in the internal channel, a sanitized verdict everywhere else. Backed by 200+ unit tests and a smoke harness that exercises the real protocol, and iterated directly from live stress-testing by working sellers.
